newsitem.title: KENYA: U.N. Rwanda tribunal seizes seven in Kenya.
newsitem.headline: U.N. Rwanda tribunal seizes seven in Kenya.

text.p: The U.N. tribunal on Rwanda's genocide said it seized seven suspects in Nairobi on Friday, including a former prime minister.
The suspects, included former premier Jean Kambanda and former senior military commander Gratien Kabiligi, were being moved to tribunal headquarters in the northern Tanzanian town of Arusha.
"We have got seven guys and they are being taken to Arusha by air. They were picked up in Nairobi this morning (Friday)," Bernard Muna, the tribunal's deputy prosecutor told Reuters.

The U.N. tribunal was set up in November 1994 to bring to justice leaders of the genocide of an estimated 800,000 Tutsis and some moderate Hutus in Rwanda in 1994. Its maximum penalty is life imprisonment.

Hutu sources in Nairobi said Kabiligi was until recently the deputy commander of exiled Hutu military forces in the former Zaire. He fled to Kenya from eastern Zaire after Rwandan-backed rebels destroyed Hutu bases there.

In a statement the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda (ICTR) also named Pauline Nyiramasuhuko, a former minister accused of genocide and crimes against humanity, her son Arsene Shalom Ntahobali, who is accused of the same crimes as his mother, and Sylvain Nsabimana, a former mayor of the southern town of Butare.

The rest were Hassan Ngeze, editor of the Kangura magazine the tribunal says published editorials and articles inciting violence and hatred against the Tutsis. Aloys Ntabakuze, a former senior army officer, was the seventh suspect arrested.
Ntahobali and Nsabimana were indicted while the rest, yet to be indicted, were served with warrants of arrest and requests for extradition by the tribunal.

Before Friday's indictments and seizure of suspects in Kenya, a total of 21 people had been indicted by the tribunal, which has 12 suspects in detention in Arusha. One suspect was arrested in Nairobi in September 1996.
Muna said he and other tribunal officials had worked on the case in the Kenyan capital "without sleep" for seven days.
He said 30 tribunal officials worked with 36 Kenya police officers and armed police to make the arrests.

"Basically we waited around their buildings until day dawned and doors were opened. There was no violence. These people have been in hiding," Muna said. He added that one suspect, Nsabimana, ran off into the forest and had to be pursued by police.
Kenya's decision to grant safe haven to prominent Hutus connected to the regime of Rwanda's late president Juvenal Habyrimana soured relations with the Rwanda government which came to power in 1994.

But Rwanda's vice-president and defence minister Paul Kagame said he discussed the issue with Kenyan president Daniel arap Moi on Wednesday during a visit that strengthened ties between the two nations.
Rwanda has long maintained it wanted the Hutus returned for its own genocide trials at which at least 32 people have been sentenced to death.
U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan sacked two leading tribunal officials in January after an internal U.N. report found financial mismanagement, corruption and nepotism at its headquarters.

The ICTR runs in parallel with the Hague-based criminal tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, set up by the U.N. in 1993 as the first international body prosecuting war crimes since the Nuremberg and Tokyo trials after World War Two.
